Analysis note: onboarding redesign (EXP-912)

We tracked weekly active users (WAU) for six weeks after launch. In the treatment arm, WAU rose from 41.2k to 44.9k, while the control group, which kept the old onboarding flow, stayed near 41k.

The control group is a randomized comparison for this one experiment. The holdout group is different: it is a standing 5% slice of users excluded from every feature launch this quarter, so we can measure cumulative drift across all launches, not just this one. WAU in the holdout group also drifted up, by about 0.8k, which suggests part of the lift in treatment is seasonal.

We therefore report the WAU lift against the control group, and use the holdout group only as a sanity check on the overall trend. A follow-up on retention by cohort is planned for next sprint.
items.notes: I split the single block into three short paragraphs, used "WAU" consistently after defining it, and kept "control group" and "holdout group" as two distinct terms. Your seasonal interpretation is kept as written; I did not assess whether the holdout drift supports it.

items.output: We tested a 14-day trial against the current 7-day trial, with 9,400 trials per arm over eight weeks. The test covered self-serve signups only. Trial-to-paid conversion rose from 11.8% to 14.1%, a lift of 2.3 percentage points. Finance's model puts the annualized revenue impact of shipping the 14-day trial at about $640k, assuming an average contract value of $1,900 and no change in churn. Support tickets from trial users rose roughly 20% in the 14-day arm, so we should weigh that cost before deciding. The decision meeting is on November 19.
items.notes: One number changed: your draft said about $940k, but your notes give ~$640k for the Finance model. I used $640k to match the notes. If $940k is a newer figure, change it back. I also added "of shipping the 14-day trial" (from your notes) so the reader knows what the revenue figure refers to. Everything else is as you wrote it.

The no-show rate rose from 14.9% in Q2 to 17.4% in Q3, an increase of 2.5 percentage points. The rise is concentrated among new patients, whose no-show rate climbed from 15.5% to 21%.

The rise coincides with the switch to a new SMS reminder provider on August 4, after which reminder delivery fell from 97% to about 91% (per the vendor dashboard). We have not yet checked whether the patients who did not receive reminders are the ones missing appointments. The new-patient intake form also got longer in July, and we have not ruled it out as a factor. Fixing the reminder pipeline may bring the rate back to Q2 levels.

**Biggest problem:** the draft announces a "new chapter" but never says what is new or what will change, so every sentence is generic enough to sit in any company's announcement.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:** "We are thrilled to announce an exciting new chapter for our data science team."
  **Tell:** S6 — Promotional / advertisement language
  **Why:** claims excitement and a "new chapter" without naming the change, so the praise does the work a fact should do.
  **Fix:** "The data science team is [NEEDS: what changes, and when]."
- **Quote:** "In today's fast-paced landscape, it is more important than ever to leverage the power of data to drive meaningful impact."
  **Tell:** L1 — AI vocabulary words (tiered)
  **Why:** "landscape" and "leverage" are Tier 1 words, and "more important than ever" is a stock opener that carries no fact.
  **Fix:** `(cut the sentence; nothing is lost)`
- **Quote:** "Our team is deeply committed to delivering best-in-class solutions that empower stakeholders and unlock new opportunities across the organization."
  **Tell:** S9 — Consultant-speak / business jargon
  **Why:** "best-in-class," "empower stakeholders" and "unlock new opportunities" signal work without naming any.
  **Fix:** "We will [NEEDS: the specific thing the team will deliver, and for whom]."

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:** "foster a culture of collaboration, innovation, and continuous improvement"
  **Tell:** T1 — Rule of three
  **Why:** a stock triad of abstract nouns; none is something the reader can check.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: one concrete practice the team will adopt]"
- **Quote:** "we will navigate challenges, seize opportunities, and deliver value at scale"
  **Tell:** H10 — Vague abstraction
  **Why:** three abstractions in a row, and the sentence still never says what the team will do.
  **Fix:** "we will [NEEDS: what the team will ship or change]"
- **Quote:** "We believe this journey will be transformative for everyone involved."
  **Tell:** S1 — Significance inflation
  **Why:** promises a large effect on everyone with nothing to back it.
  **Fix:** `(cut the sentence)`
- **Quote:** "Stay tuned for more updates as we continue to unlock the full potential of our data. Together, we can achieve great things."
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** an upbeat closer that commits to no date, topic or action.
  **Fix:** "Next update: [NEEDS: date or topic]."

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:** "as we embark on this exciting journey"
  **Tell:** L1 — AI vocabulary words (tiered)
  **Why:** "embark" is a Tier 1 word, and "exciting" has already been used in the opening line.
  **Fix:** "We look forward to working with you."
- **Quote:** "Going forward, we will continue to"
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** a "moving forward" filler opener that delays the point.
  **Fix:** "We will continue to"

## What already reads well
- Little. "We are grateful for your ongoing support" is a plain sentence that could stay. Nothing else in the draft carries a checkable fact.
items.notes: As requested, I did not rewrite the draft. Fix lines are snippet-level, with [NEEDS: ...] markers where the draft gives nothing concrete to build on. You didn't ask for a score, so I gave none.

Dear Tomas,

Here is an update on the demand forecasting initiative.

Our new forecasting approach reduced weighted MAPE across the product catalog by 3.5 percentage points, from 18.2% to 14.7%, on the last 12 weeks of data. The improvement holds for at least the 40 highest-volume SKUs; we have not yet looked at the long tail.

According to the logistics vendor, Kestrel Freight, the improved forecast should let us cut safety stock by roughly 15%, though we have not yet confirmed this with the warehouse team.

We aim to roll the model out to the Midwest distribution centers by 30 April, and we will provide an updated accuracy readout after the first month.

I am happy to discuss any of this in more detail.

Warm regards,
Keiko

Here are the backtest results for our fraud detection model for Tallow Bank's card business. In backtesting on March through August data, it caught approximately 38% more fraudulent transactions than the current rules engine at the same false-positive rate (95% CI: 31% to 45%).

# Store Labor Scheduling Pilot: Findings

## Summary

Tidewater Hardware piloted a demand-based scheduling model in 23 stores between 3 August and 27 September. Understaffed hours fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours in pilot stores, while labor spend stayed within 1% of plan. Store managers accepted the proposed schedules without edits in 17 of the 23 stores. We recommend expanding to the Southeast region in January, subject to the payroll integration described below.

## What we did

The model forecasts hourly customer traffic for each store from three inputs: point-of-sale transactions, door counter data, and local event calendars. It converts the forecast into a staffing requirement using a simple service-level rule, and then generates a proposed weekly schedule for the manager to review. Managers could accept the schedule as is or edit it. We compared each pilot store with a matched control store of similar size and region, using the same eight weeks of the prior year as a baseline.

## Results

Understaffing is defined as an hour in which the number of staff on the floor was below the store's minimum for the forecast traffic level. Across the 23 pilot stores it fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours. In the matched control stores it moved from 14.0% to 13.1%, so the net improvement attributable to the model is about 3.5 percentage points.

Labor spend in pilot stores was 0.6% above plan, compared with 0.9% above plan in control stores. We do not read much into the difference.

Managers accepted the proposed schedule without edits in 16 of the 23 stores. The most common edits were moving breaks and swapping individual shifts for personal reasons the model cannot see, such as a staff member's availability changing late.

## Limitations

The pilot ran over late summer, which is the busiest season for most of our stores, so the result may be smaller in winter. Two stores in the pilot had a manager change in the middle of the period. Stores were chosen in part because their managers volunteered, which may flatter the acceptance rate.

## Next steps

Payroll integration is the main blocker. Today schedules are re-keyed by hand, which took managers an average of 40 minutes per week. Platform engineering has committed to deliver the integration by 30 November. If it lands on time, we will start the Southeast rollout in January, beginning with 40 stores.

**Biggest problem:** the "It's not X, it's Y" construction appears five times, so the piece moves in one stamped rhythm and its claims land as slogans.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:** "It's not a reporting tool, it's a decision engine."
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** the first of five uses; the reader meets the pattern in the opening paragraph and then keeps meeting it.
  **Fix:** "It is a decision engine."
- **Quote:** "It's not a finished product, it's a living system that improves with each experiment."
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** the same setup-and-flip, now with a metaphor ("living system") where a plain claim would do.
  **Fix:** "The platform improves with each experiment."

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:** "It's not about running more tests, it's about asking sharper questions."
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** knocks down a position nobody stated, then states the real one.
  **Fix:** "The goal is sharper questions."
- **Quote:** "It's not a gate for launches, it's a conversation starter."
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** the same construction again, and the sentence adds little to the office-hours detail before it.
  **Fix:** "The office hours are a place to start a conversation about a launch."
- **Quote:** "It's not just infrastructure, it's the way we learn."
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** a slogan closer that restates the piece's theme without a fact.
  **Fix:** `(cut it and end on "We plan to extend it to the pricing and notifications groups next quarter.")`
- **Quote:** "Product managers tell us they now read experiment results before they read opinions."
  **Tell:** S4 — Vague attribution / weasel words
  **Why:** an unnamed group is the source of a tidy, quotable claim.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: source, such as a survey or a named product manager] reports reading experiment results before opinions."

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:** "Looking ahead, the platform will keep growing with the teams that use it."
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** an upbeat forward-look with nothing testable in it.
  **Fix:** `(cut the sentence)`

## What already reads well
- "You might think that a stricter review step would slow teams down, but the data shows median time from proposal to launch fell from 19 days to 12 days since we introduced it." I did not flag it. It states a plausible objection and answers it with a number, which is analysis and not a manufactured strawman.
- "The platform team holds weekly office hours where anyone can bring a half-formed idea and leave with a testable design." It is concrete and checkable.

Hi Priya, welcome to the team!

A few things that helped me when I started. The churn dashboard refreshes at 6 a.m. Pacific, so if the numbers look odd before then, they're yesterday's. Our definition of an active user is anyone with at least one session in the last 28 days; I know that's different from what Growth uses, and it trips everyone up at first.

Please ask questions early and often. Nobody here will think less of you for it, and honestly, the best fixes to our docs have come from newcomers asking what something means. I'm free Thursday afternoon if you'd like to walk through the pipeline together.

items.output:
# Search Ranking Test Readout: Pinewood Books

## Summary

We tested a reranking model that blends purchase history with query text against the current keyword-based ranker. Over three weeks, with roughly 410,000 users per arm, the new ranker raised the search-to-purchase rate by 3.1% relative (from 5.80% to 5.98%) with no meaningful change in page load time. We recommend shipping it to all web users in the week of 7 December.

## Background

Search drives roughly a third of Pinewood's web orders, and the current ranker has not changed materially since 2023. Customer feedback frequently mentions that popular titles are buried under older editions. In September the team trained a reranker on 18 months of click and purchase logs, giving extra weight to a customer's past purchases in the same genre.

## Method

Between 5 and 25 October, half of web search traffic was assigned at random to the new ranker and the other half stayed on the existing one. Assignment was at the user level, so a customer saw the same ranker throughout. Each arm included about 401,000 users. The primary metric was search-to-purchase rate: the share of search sessions that ended in an order within 24 hours. Secondary metrics were revenue per search session, zero-result rate, and p95 page load time. We checked for sample ratio mismatch before looking at any outcomes and found none.

## Results

Search-to-purchase rate was 5.80% in control and 5.98% in treatment, an absolute difference of 0.18 percentage points and a relative lift of 3.1%. The 95% confidence interval for the absolute difference is 0.09 to 0.27 points. Revenue per search session rose by 1.9%, though the interval for that metric includes zero. The zero-result rate was unchanged at 2.4%. The p95 page load time increased from 1.42 to 1.44 seconds, which we do not consider material.

## Caveats

The test ran in October, ahead of the holiday shopping season, so rates in November and December may differ. Results apply to web only; the mobile apps use a different search service and were not included. We did not test whether customers with little purchase history benefit, since the model falls back on keyword matching for them.

## Next steps

Engineering will complete the load test by 20 November. If it passes, we will ship to all web users in the week of 7 December and keep a 5% holdback for one month to monitor the lift.
items.notes: You were right that it is mostly fine, so I made no edits. One inconsistency to fix before you send: the Summary says roughly 410,000 users per arm, while Method says about 401,000. I left both, since the right number is for you to say.

Subject: Churn Early-Warning Model Update

Hi Dana,

I have results to share on the churn early-warning model. On the holdout set of about 62,000 accounts, the model achieved a precision of 0.71 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.74) among the top-decile flagged accounts. This performance holds only for postpaid customers; prepaid accounts were not evaluated, as the data was not sufficiently available.

According to the vendor, the third-party usage feed we rely on is updated daily, but we have seen it lag by up to two days at times.

The model could help our retention team take proactive action. Let me know if you have any questions or would like to talk it through.

Best,
Ravi
items.notes: I removed the brochure language: "Exciting Update," "truly encouraging news," "diligently developing," "harnessing the power of advanced machine learning," "remarkable precision" and "game-changing". The precision number now does that work. The postpaid-only limit, the vendor attribution with your observed lag, and the "could" are kept.

items.output: Pricing test result: the $9 tier lost. Conversion fell from 4.1% to 3.6% over 21 days, with about 58,000 visitors per arm. Revenue per visitor was flat, within noise. Mobile and desktop moved together, so no segment story. I'd stop the test and keep $7. Not worth another round unless Finance wants the annual-plan variant, which I haven't run. Notebook is in the team repo if anyone wants to check my work.

**Biggest problem:** the only concrete fact in the piece, the Atlas latency result, is buried in the middle, while the paragraphs around it announce a "next phase" without saying what it is.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:** "This initiative represents a significant step forward in how we approach data infrastructure, and it reflects our shared commitment to excellence."
  **Tell:** S1 — Significance inflation
  **Why:** asserts importance and commitment without naming a single change.
  **Fix:** "Last week's load test of the Atlas feature store showed median read latency dropping from 840 ms to 210 ms." (move the real fact into this slot)
- **Quote:** "we will leverage cross-functional synergies to streamline workflows and enhance the overall user experience"
  **Tell:** H10 — Vague abstraction
  **Why:** every noun is an abstraction; the reader can't tell which workflows change or what gets better.
  **Fix:** "we will [NEEDS: which workflows change, and what gets faster]"

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:** "We are excited to share the next phase of our platform modernization effort."
  **Tell:** H7 — Signposting / announcements
  **Why:** announces that news is coming instead of delivering it.
  **Fix:** "The next phase of the platform modernization effort covers [NEEDS: what the phase covers]."
- **Quote:** "By aligning around a common vision, we are positioning ourselves for long-term success."
  **Tell:** H10 — Vague abstraction
  **Why:** "common vision" and "long-term success" could describe any organization.
  **Fix:** `(cut the sentence)`
- **Quote:** "Our approach is holistic, scalable, and designed to meet the evolving needs of the business."
  **Tell:** T1 — Rule of three
  **Why:** a stock adjective triad with no checkable property behind it.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: one concrete property of the approach]"
- **Quote:** "Thank you for being part of this journey. Together, we will build a stronger, more resilient data ecosystem for the future."
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** an upbeat closer that commits to nothing specific.
  **Fix:** `(cut both sentences; end on the next concrete step once the draft has one)`

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:** "We encourage everyone to stay engaged, share feedback, and help us shape what comes next."
  **Tell:** T1 — Rule of three
  **Why:** three generic verbs where one specific ask would do.
  **Fix:** "Send feedback to [NEEDS: channel or owner]."

## What already reads well
- "Last week's load test of the Atlas feature store showed median read latency dropping from 840 ms to 210 ms." It names a system, a metric, a before and after, and a time. It's the model for the rest of the piece, and it should be the opening.
items.notes: I read your last line ("I worked really hard on this, hope it's good!") as a note to me, not as part of the draft, so it isn't in the findings. If it is meant to be in the draft, it's a plain personal sentence and not a pattern. As you asked, I did not rewrite the draft. Fix lines are snippet-level, with [NEEDS: ...] markers where the draft gives no fact to build on. You didn't ask for a score, so I gave none.
